passages.text: EARTHQUAKE, a violent agitation or trembling of some considerable part of the earth, generally attended with a terrible noise like thunder, and sometimes with an eruption of fire, water or wind.
The cause is commonly ascribed to subterraneous fires, or to vapours and exhalations which, being rarefied by heat and wanting room, burst forth with violence and shake the ground above them.
Dr Stukeley has supposed that earthquakes are owing to electricity, the shock being communicated through the earth as through other conductors.
They are most frequent in countries abounding with volcanoes, as Italy, Sicily, and the islands of the Indian ocean.
The most dreadful of late years was that which destroyed great part of Lisbon on the first of November 1755, when many thousands of the inhabitants perished.
An earthquake is the shaking of the Earth's surface caused by a sudden release of energy in the lithosphere that creates seismic waves.

Most earthquakes happen when rock breaks and slips along a geological fault, as the tectonic plates move against each other. Volcanic activity and human activity, such as mining, cause smaller earthquakes.
Earthquakes concentrate along the boundaries of tectonic plates, such as the Pacific Ring of Fire, where many volcanoes also form.
Seismometers record seismic waves. The size of an earthquake is reported on the moment magnitude scale.
The 1755 Lisbon earthquake, followed by a tsunami and fires, killed tens of thousands of people and is often seen as the start of the scientific study of earthquakes.
Earthquakes under the sea can cause tsunamis.

reasons: The article on the Lisbon earthquake scores close behind but covers one event only.

alignments.label: What an earthquake is

britannica.quote: a violent agitation or trembling of some considerable part of the earth

wikipedia.quote: the shaking of the Earth's surface

alignments.note: The same event in plainer words. Wikipedia adds what travels through the ground: seismic waves.

alignments.label: The cause

britannica.quote: commonly ascribed to subterraneous fires, or to vapours and exhalations

wikipedia.quote: rock breaks and slips along a geological fault

alignments.note: Underground fire and trapped vapour gave way to moving plates and breaking rock.

alignments.label: Earthquakes as electricity
alignments.note: Stukeley’s electrical theory has no place in the modern account.

alignments.label: Near volcanoes

britannica.quote: most frequent in countries abounding with volcanoes

alignments.note: The pattern was right, the reason was not: earthquakes and volcanoes both follow plate boundaries.

alignments.label: Lisbon, 1755

britannica.quote: destroyed great part of Lisbon on the first of November 1755

alignments.note: Recent news in 1797, and the start of earthquake science today.

alignments.label: Measuring them
alignments.note: In 1797 there was no way to measure an earthquake, only to describe its damage.

suggestedQuestions: What did people in 1797 think caused earthquakes?
Was the 1797 entry right that earthquakes happen near volcanoes?

What did people in 1797 think caused ear.answer:
Most blamed "subterraneous fires, or vapours and exhalations" that burst out and shook the ground [B2]. Dr Stukeley proposed electricity instead [B3].

Wikipedia explains earthquakes as rock breaking and slipping along faults as tectonic plates move [W2]. Neither 1797 cause survives.

Was the 1797 entry right that earthquake.answer:
Partly. It says earthquakes are most frequent where volcanoes abound [B4], and Wikipedia agrees that both cluster along plate boundaries such as the Ring of Fire [W3].

The pattern was right, but the entry took it as cause and effect. Today both are seen as results of moving plates [W2].
